meta.basis: NEC 2020 (Florida Building Code, 8th Edition). Plain-language summaries in our own words — not NFPA text.
meta.status: PLACEHOLDER entries — Mike Holt's content files replace these; every entry is draft until he checks it.

topics.title: Box fill
topics.summary: Every conductor, clamp, device and ground takes up space in the box, counted in cubic inches by wire size. Count each current-carrying and insulated conductor once, all grounds together as one, internal clamps as one, and each device yoke as two (based on the largest wire on that device). Compare the total against the box's marked volume or Table 314.16(A).

topics.title: Conductor ampacity
topics.summary: Ampacity comes from Table 310.16 by wire size, material and insulation temperature rating; most terminations limit you to the 75°C column. For small conductors, 240.4(D) caps the breaker: 14 AWG copper tops out at 15A, 12 AWG at 20A, 10 AWG at 30A no matter what the table column says. CCA (copper-clad aluminum) sizes like aluminum in the table — one AWG up from copper for the same breaker (Sharma rule SR-7).

topics.title: Conduit fill
topics.summary: Conductors may fill at most 53% of a conduit's internal area for one conductor, 31% for two, and 40% for three or more. Use conductor areas from Table 5 and conduit areas from Table 4. Equipment grounds count as conductors for fill.

topics.title: Voltage drop
topics.summary: Not a hard code limit, but the code's informational notes recommend no more than 3% drop on a branch circuit and 5% total for feeder plus branch. Long runs need bigger wire: VD = 2 × K × I × L ÷ circular mils (K = 12.9 copper, 21.2 aluminum). Use the calculator in this app.

topics.title: Branch circuits & receptacle spacing
topics.summary: Along a wall, no point may be more than 6 ft from a receptacle, so spacing is 12 ft apart maximum, and any wall run 2 ft or wider gets one. Hallways 10 ft or longer need at least one receptacle. Kitchens, bathrooms, laundry and garages each have their own required circuits — see the room checklists.

topics.title: AFCI & GFCI protection
topics.summary: GFCI protects people from shock in wet and risky locations: bathrooms, kitchens, garages, outdoors, laundry, basements and more. AFCI protects against arc faults in living areas — bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, laundry and similar rooms. Sharma rule: every 120V breaker is dual-function AFCI/GFCI, so both protections live at the breaker.

topics.title: Service & panel working clearances
topics.summary: Electrical equipment needs working space: at least 3 ft deep in front, 30 in wide (or the equipment width if wider), and 6.5 ft of headroom. That space stays clear — it is not storage. Panels in homes also cannot go in bathrooms or over stair steps.

topics.title: Grounding & bonding
topics.summary: Grounding connects the system to earth through the grounding electrode system (rods, water pipe, concrete-encased electrode); bonding connects metal parts together so faults trip the breaker fast. The main bonding jumper ties neutral to ground at the service only — never downstream. Keep grounds and neutrals separated in subpanels.

topics.title: Service & feeder sizing
topics.summary: For a house, the optional method of 220.82 is the usual path: general lighting at 3 VA per square foot, 1,500 VA each for the small-appliance and laundry circuits, nameplate ratings for appliances, then demand factors on the total, plus the larger of heating or cooling. Use the load calculator in this app, then confirm against the service size.

topics.title: Pools & spas
topics.summary: Pools have their own world: equipotential bonding of everything metal near the water, GFCI protection for receptacles and equipment, strict distances for receptacles (6 ft minimum from the water's edge for general receptacles) and for overhead lines. Never treat pool work like ordinary outdoor work.

topics.title: Solar PV
topics.summary: Solar systems need listed disconnects, rapid shutdown for rooftop arrays, proper labeling at every disconnect and the service, and the 120% rule when backfeeding a panel busbar (705.12): the sum of breaker ratings feeding the bus cannot exceed 120% of the bus rating.

topics.title: EV chargers
topics.summary: EV charging is a continuous load — size the branch circuit at 125% of the charger's rating. A 48A charger needs a 60A circuit. The load also counts at 100% (or 7,200 VA minimum) in service load calculations.

topics.title: Generators & transfer switches
topics.summary: Optional standby systems must use a transfer switch or interlock so the generator can never backfeed the utility. Permanently installed generators need a disconnect and clear labeling; portable generator connections need a listed inlet and interlock or transfer equipment. Never a male-to-male cord, ever.

topics.title: Smoke & CO alarms
topics.summary: Florida requires smoke alarms inside every bedroom, outside each sleeping area, and on every level; CO alarms where fuel-burning appliances or attached garages exist. In new work they are hardwired, interconnected, with battery backup. Placement on ceilings or high on walls, away from kitchens and bathrooms that cause false alarms.

topics.title: HVAC disconnects
topics.summary: AC equipment needs a disconnect within sight of the unit, sized from the nameplate: branch-circuit protection follows the nameplate MAX fuse/breaker, and conductors follow the nameplate MIN circuit ampacity. The nameplate wins over generic tables — always read MCA and MOCP off the unit.
